meta.name: Mini Goldendoodle
meta.tagline: The Mini Goldendoodle is a Golden Retriever crossed with a Miniature Poodle, usually through F1B or multigenerational breeding. GANA defines a mini as 14–17 inches and typically 26–35 lbs, but a puppy's adult size is an educated guess, and the Golden side's health risks don't shrink with the dog.
meta.excerpt: A Mini Goldendoodle is a Golden Retriever–Miniature Poodle cross that GANA sizes at 14–17 inches and about 26–35 lbs, though a puppy's adult size is an educated guess. Here's what differs from a standard Goldendoodle and which health tests to ask for.
meta.meta_description: Mini Goldendoodle guide: how minis are bred, why adult size is hard to predict, F1 vs F1B coats, GANA health tests, grooming needs, and cost ranges.

intro.label: Overview
intro.heading: What Is a Mini Goldendoodle?
intro.html:
A Mini Goldendoodle is a Golden Retriever crossed with a Miniature Poodle. It's the same idea as the full-size Goldendoodle, a friendly retriever temperament plus a Poodle-type coat, scaled down to a dog most people can pick up. It isn't an AKC breed, so there's no AKC breed standard and no required health testing, although mixed and designer dogs can enroll in AKC sports through the AKC Canine Partners program. The main breed club is the Goldendoodle Association of North America (GANA). Its standard limits the Goldendoodle to Poodles and Golden Retrievers, keeps the stud book open, and sets the size classes and health-testing tiers this guide refers to.

Getting a small dog from these two parents takes some engineering. AKC standards put a Golden Retriever at 55–75 lbs and a Miniature Poodle at 10–15 lbs, roughly a four- to six-fold difference. Breeders describe two common routes. A first-generation (F1) mini usually has a Golden Retriever mother and a Miniature Poodle father, often bred by artificial insemination. More often, breeders cross an F1 Goldendoodle back to a Miniature Poodle (an F1B, about 75% Poodle by pedigree) or breed Mini Goldendoodles to each other over several generations (multigen). These are breeder practices rather than rules, so ask exactly how your puppy's litter was produced.

This page covers what's different about the mini: how predictable adult size really is, what the extra Poodle ancestry does to the coat, the small-dog health problems to screen for, and what one costs. For generations, temperament and the Golden Retriever side in more depth, read our Goldendoodle guide.

appearance.label: Physical
appearance.heading: Size, Coat and Looks
appearance.html:
GANA sorts Goldendoodles into four size classes by adult height. The weights are typical ranges, not cut-offs:

GANA classHeight at the withersTypical weight
PetiteUnder 14 in25 lbs or less
MiniatureOver 14 in, under 17 in26–35 lbs
MediumOver 17 in, under 21 in36–50 lbs
StandardOver 21 in51 lbs or more

Advertisements use “mini” more loosely. Some sellers' size charts stretch a mini up to 45 lbs, which is GANA's medium class. GANA itself says a dog's final size class is decided at adulthood and that a breeder's estimate for a puppy is an “educated guess.” Before you pay extra for small, ask for both parents' adult heights and weights, the generation of the litter, and which GANA class the breeder expects your puppy to land in.

Coats run from flat to wavy to curly. Research on purebred dogs found that variants in just three genes explain most coat types: RSPO2 (the beard and eyebrows, called furnishings), FGF5 (coat length) and KRT71 (curl). The more Poodle ancestry a puppy has, the better its odds of inheriting the Poodle versions, which is why F1B and multigen minis tend to have more uniform wavy-to-curly coats than F1s. A genetic study of multigenerational Australian Labradoodles, a similar cross, found the breed was mostly Poodle at the genome level and enriched for the Poodle coat variants that breeders believe make a dog hypoallergenic. A Poodle-type coat isn't the same as an allergen-free dog, though (see the FAQ).

GANA's standard accepts any coat color except those tied to health problems, such as double merle, double dilute and extreme white that can affect hearing. A double merle comes from breeding two merle dogs together, so ask about both parents' colors if a breeder advertises merle puppies. It's also worth asking whether the parents have had coat-gene DNA tests, which can help a breeder predict a puppy's coat.

temperament.label: Personality
temperament.heading: Temperament
temperament.html:
GANA's breed standard asks for a Goldendoodle that is friendly, reliable, trustworthy and well-rounded, and says dogs that are hostile, timid, nervous or hyperactive shouldn't be bred. The parents' reputations point the same way: the AKC describes the Golden Retriever as intelligent, friendly and devoted, and the Miniature Poodle as active, proud and very smart. In practice that usually adds up to a social, people-focused dog that wants to be part of whatever its family is doing.

Breed labels only go so far, though. In a study of more than 18,000 dogs, breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. With a cross, the parents you can meet tell you more than the word “doodle” does. Meet the mother at least, ask how the litter is being socialized, and ask the breeder to match a puppy's energy level to your household.

Two things catch new owners out. The first is alone time: start practicing short absences early, and read the separation-anxiety FAQ in our Goldendoodle guide, which applies to minis too. The second is upkeep. In a U.S. survey of 2,191 dog owners, more than twice as many doodle owners as other owners said grooming and other maintenance took more work than they had expected. With children, a 26–35 lb dog is sturdier than a toy breed but can still knock over a toddler, so supervise play and teach kids not to grab or hug the dog.

mikes_take.label: A Realistic Take
mikes_take.heading: What I'd Tell a Friend Thinking About a Mini Goldendoodle
mikes_take.html:
If you want the Goldendoodle personality in a dog you can carry up the stairs, the mini makes a lot of sense. Just know which part of the market you're shopping in. Much of what you'll read online, from size charts to “hypoallergenic” promises, comes from people with puppies to sell.

Treat “mini” as a forecast, not a promise. I'd want to see both parents' adult weights, know the generation, and get the breeder's expected GANA size class in writing. If a weight limit really matters, say for a lease or a building rule, an adult from a doodle rescue whose size is already known is the safer bet.

Smaller doesn't mean fewer health tests. You're adding the Miniature Poodle side's small-dog problems, like slipping kneecaps and dental disease, to the Golden side's hips, elbows, eyes, heart and high cancer rate. GANA's entry-level Bronze tier doesn't require elbows or an eye exam, so ask for those results whatever the badge says, and look every result up yourself on ofa.org.

Finally, budget for grooming the way you would for a full-size doodle. It's the same coat with the same appointments, just on a smaller dog. If what you mainly want is a small, curly-coated dog of predictable size, a purebred Miniature Poodle deserves a serious look.

care.label: Daily Life
care.heading: Care Requirements
care.html:
Exercise

Plan on 45–60 minutes a day of walks and active play. Both parents were bred to work. The AKC says Goldens, like most sporting breeds, need plenty of daily exercise and tend to misbehave without it, and that Poodles of any size are very active dogs that need good exercise every day. Both were bred to retrieve, and the AKC notes that most Poodles love the water. Shorter legs don't mean a smaller engine.

Mental Stimulation

Short daily training sessions, puzzle feeders, scent games and trick training all suit a mini. A bored, clever dog invents its own hobbies, and they usually involve your shoes or your sofa.

Grooming

Professional grooming every 6–8 weeks, plus brushing all the way to the skin several times a week at home, and daily during the change from puppy to adult coat. Wavy and curly coats mat wherever things rub: behind the ears, under the collar and in the armpits. Brush teeth daily if you can.

Check the ears weekly and dry them after swimming or baths. Drop ears raise the risk of outer-ear infections (otitis externa). In UK veterinary records, breeds with hanging ears had 1.76 times the odds of breeds with upright ears, Poodle types had 1.91 times the odds of non-Poodle types, and Golden Retrievers had 2.23 times the odds of crossbred dogs. Full routine in our Goldendoodle grooming guide.

Training

Minis usually learn quickly and respond well to reward-based training. Start early on three things: short practice absences, polite greetings, and daily handling of paws, ears and face so groomer visits aren't a fight. A puppy class gives you socialization and structure at the same time. Our Goldendoodle puppy checklist covers the first weeks at home.

health.label: Wellness
health.heading: Health & Common Conditions
health.html:
No study has looked at Mini Goldendoodle health specifically, so plan for the risks of both parents. The best evidence on Poodle crosses comes from a 2024 UK owner survey of 9,402 dogs that compared Cockapoos, Labradoodles and Cavapoos with their parent breeds. In 86.6% of 342 disorder comparisons, the cross was no different from its parent breed. Labradoodles, the closest relative to a Goldendoodle in that study, matched Poodles on 50 of 57 disorders. The authors found little support for the idea that these crosses are healthier because they're crosses, so testing the parents still matters.

ConditionWhat It Means
Patellar LuxationThe kneecap slips out of its groove. The American College of Veterinary Surgeons calls it one of the most common orthopedic problems in dogs, diagnosed in 7% of puppies, and lists miniature poodles among the predisposed small breeds. A classic sign is a dog that suddenly skips or carries a hind leg for a few steps. GANA requires an OFA patella clearance for Poodle and Goldendoodle parents of every size.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes DiseaseThe blood supply to the top of the thigh bone fails in a young dog and the bone breaks down. The Orthopedic Foundation for Animals (OFA) says it's most often seen in miniature and toy breeds, Poodles among them, between 4 months and 1 year of age. A young mini that limps on a hind leg needs a vet visit. OFA says a dog over 12 months with a normal OFA hip result is also normal for LCP, so the parents' OFA hip clearances double as an LCP screen.
Hip & Elbow DysplasiaMalformed joints that lead to arthritis, mainly a concern from the Golden side. The Golden Retriever Club of America (GRCA) asks its breeders for OFA or PennHIP hip results and OFA elbow results at 24 months or older. GANA requires hips at every tier (OFA Fair or better), but elbows only at Silver and Gold.
Progressive Retinal Atrophy & Other Eye DiseasePRA causes gradual vision loss that ends in blindness. GANA's Bronze tier requires DNA tests for prcd-PRA and the Golden-specific GR-PRA1 and GR-PRA2, but an eye exam by a veterinary ophthalmologist (CAER) every two years only at Gold. The GRCA asks for an eye exam within 12 months before each breeding.
Heart DiseaseThe GRCA asks for a heart exam by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist at 12 months or older. GANA requires a cardiac clearance for Golden Retriever and Goldendoodle parents (not Poodles).
CancerThe Golden side's biggest risk. In the GRCA's 1998–99 health survey of 1,444 Goldens, cancer caused 61.4% of the deaths a vet confirmed, and the estimated lifetime risk was about 1 in 5 for hemangiosarcoma and 1 in 8 for lymphoma. Nobody has measured whether crossing to a Miniature Poodle, or a smaller body, changes that, so don't assume it does. Have your vet check any new lump promptly.
Dental DiseaseIn UK veterinary records, the odds of gum (periodontal) disease rose steadily as adult bodyweight fell; the Toy Poodle had the highest odds of any breed (3.97 times crossbreds), while Golden Retrievers and Labradoodles showed no raised odds. Small Poodle crosses need daily brushing and regular dental checkups.
Leg Length & Disc Disease (CDPA/CDDY)GANA lists two optional DNA tests: chondrodysplasia/chondrodystrophy (CDPA/CDDY), the short-leg variants, offered only for toy, mini and medium Poodle and Goldendoodle lines, and intervertebral disc disease (IVDD type 1). CDDY is linked to early disc degeneration in many breeds, but GANA says it hasn't yet seen an association with disc disease in Goldendoodles and recommends the test so it can keep monitoring. Neither test is required at any tier, so ask whether the parents were tested.

Ask breeders for (both parents): The GANA membership logo with kennel name, year joined, testing tier and a valid expiration date. OFA hips and patellas; OFA elbows and a CAER eye exam from the last two years even if the breeder is Bronze; a cardiac clearance on the Golden or Goldendoodle parent; and DNA results for prcd-PRA, GR-PRA1, GR-PRA2, ichthyosis (ICH1), NEwS, von Willebrand disease type 1 and degenerative myelopathy. These are recessive, so a puppy can only be affected if both parents carry the same variant; GANA's rules limit which carriers can be paired. CDDY and IVDD results are a bonus. Look every result up yourself on ofa.org.

cost.label: Budget
cost.heading: Cost of Ownership
cost.html:
There's no survey of Mini Goldendoodle prices. Every figure below is an estimated range from a named source. The puppy line uses PetMD's Goldendoodle range of $1,500–$5,000, which it says varies by breeder, size and lineage; for comparison, Rover's 2026 data puts breeder costs across all breeds at $675–$4,440. The other lines come from Rover's 2026 cost-of-dog-ownership figures, which cover dogs of every size. Rover notes that small-breed adults can cost up to 63% less a year than large and giant breeds, so a 26–35 lb mini will usually land below the middle of the food, gear and insurance ranges. Grooming is based on Thumbtack's national per-session averages.

Rover's annual breakdown has no line for professional grooming, so add the grooming line on top. It assumes 6.5 to 8.7 appointments a year at Thumbtack's $79–$136 average session prices, and smaller dogs usually cost less per visit than big ones. For insurance context, the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA) reports an average U.S. accident-and-illness premium for dogs of $836 in 2025; your quote will depend on age, location and plan. Read the policy's rules on hereditary conditions and orthopedic waiting periods before you enroll, since kneecaps and hips are the likely claims. For a line-by-line budget, see our Goldendoodle first-year costs; minis sit at the low end of most lines.

right_for_you.label: Fit Assessment
right_for_you.heading: Is a Mini Goldendoodle Right for You?
good_fit: Families and apartment dwellers who want Goldendoodle friendliness in a 26–35 lb dog
Active people who'll give a small dog 45–60 minutes of exercise plus daily training
Owners who can budget roughly $515–$1,185 a year for professional grooming, for life
Buyers willing to wait for a breeder who shows OFA results for both parents
Households where someone is home much of the day, or that can arrange midday company
not_fit: Anyone who needs a guaranteed adult size; a puppy's size estimate is an educated guess
Allergy sufferers relying on a “hypoallergenic” label
Owners who want a low-maintenance coat; grooming is the same as for a full-size doodle
Buyers shopping mainly on price, or for a puppy that can ship this week
People who want a calm lap dog; both parents are active working breeds

finding.label: Next Steps
finding.heading: Finding Your Mini Goldendoodle
finding.html:
Buying from a Breeder

Start with GANA's member breeder directory, which you can filter by size and health-testing level. GANA says genuine members display a custom logo with their kennel name, the year they joined, their testing level (Bronze, Silver or Gold) and a valid expiration date, and that any other logo isn't proof of membership. Check the health-testing standards so you know what each tier covers. Then ask to see the OFA certificates for both parents, look them up on ofa.org, and ask for the elbow and eye results that Bronze doesn't require. A good breeder will tell you plainly which generation the litter is, what the parents weigh, and how confident they are about adult size.

For a benchmark of what purebred clubs expect from their own breeders, see the Golden Retriever Club of America's breeder guidance and the Poodle Club of America's breeder referral. Our guide on how to find a responsible breeder explains how to verify health claims step by step.

Red Flags

  • A guaranteed adult size for a young puppy, or “micro” and “teacup” labels
  • “Hybrid vigor, so we don't need to test”
  • No OFA numbers you can look up, or results for only one parent
  • A deposit demanded before a video call or visit, or a puppy shipped sight unseen; see our guide to puppy scams

Rescue

Doodle rescues are worth checking, but minis are scarce. IDOG Rescue, a national foster-based doodle rescue founded in 2006, says it has placed more than 3,000 doodles, but that mini doodles are uncommon in its program. Its adoption FAQ lists fees of $100–$750 depending on the dog, while its adoption page says up to $1,000, so confirm the fee for the dog you're interested in. Petfinder and Adopt a Pet let you search shelters by breed. An adult's size and coat are already settled, which removes the two biggest guesses with a mini. Our guide to adopting vs. buying a dog walks through the trade-offs.

Bringing a puppy home? Work through the Goldendoodle puppy checklist, and read our look at doodle breeding ethics and the best Doodle breeds for families if you're still deciding.

faq.q: How big do Mini Goldendoodles get?
faq.a: GANA's Miniature class is over 14 and under 17 inches at the withers, typically 26–35 lbs. Under 14 inches (usually 25 lbs or less) is Petite, and 17–21 inches (36–50 lbs) is Medium. Some sellers' “mini” charts run as high as 45 lbs. Final size is only known at adulthood, and GANA calls a breeder's estimate for a puppy an educated guess. The parents' adult weights and the litter's generation are your best clues.

faq.q: What's the difference between an F1 and an F1B Mini Goldendoodle?
faq.a: An F1 is a first-generation cross of a Golden Retriever and a Miniature Poodle. An F1B is an F1 Goldendoodle bred back to a Miniature Poodle, so it's about 75% Poodle by pedigree. Multigen minis come from Goldendoodles bred together over several generations. More Poodle ancestry makes a wavy or curly coat and a smaller size more likely, but no generation guarantees either.

No dog is reliably hypoallergenic. In a Dutch study, dogs commonly called hypoallergenic, including Labradoodles and Poodles, had higher levels of the main dog allergen (Can f 1) in hair and coat samples than other dogs, and airborne allergen levels in their homes were no different. A U.S. study of house dust also found no difference between homes with “hypoallergenic” and other dogs. A curly, low-shedding coat may leave less hair around the house, but that isn't the same as less allergen. If someone in your home has dog allergies, talk to an allergist and spend time with the parents or an adult dog before you commit.

faq.q: How long do Mini Goldendoodles live?
faq.a: No study has measured it. PetMD gives Goldendoodles 10–15 years and says Mini Goldendoodles typically live longer than large ones. The AKC gives Golden Retrievers 10–12 years and Miniature Poodles 10–18 years, and large UK studies find that heavier dogs tend to have shorter lives. 10–15 years is a reasonable estimate, not a measured figure, and nobody knows whether the Golden side's high cancer rate is any lower in minis.

faq.q: Mini vs. standard Goldendoodle: what's actually different?
faq.a: Mainly size: GANA's mini class is typically 26–35 lbs versus 51 lbs or more for a standard. Minis have a Miniature Poodle parent and are often F1B or multigen, so small-dog problems like slipping kneecaps, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease and dental disease matter more. Food and grooming cost a bit less. Coat care is the same, exercise needs are only somewhat lower, and the Golden Retriever cancer risk is shared.

faq.q: Are Mini Goldendoodles good apartment dogs?
faq.a: Their size suits an apartment, but their energy and social needs are the real test. Plan on 45–60 minutes of exercise a day, daily training or games, and not leaving the dog alone for a full workday. If you can provide that, a mini can do well in a small home.
